inevitable

/in-EV-ih-tuh-bul/ — stress EV: 'in-EV-itable' · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Inevitable is certain to happen; impossible to avoid.

Once the ship's hull cracked, sinking became inevitable.

Example

The old dam had cracked years ago, and every spring the crack widened. Engineers warned that no repair could hold and that a breach was inevitable — one day the water would break through no matter what anyone did.

Inevitable means certain to happen and impossible to avoid. A 'likely' event will probably occur; an inevitable one cannot be escaped at all.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

unavoidable: Unavoidable means impossible to escape or prevent, and it is the plainest of these words — a fee or a delay can be unavoidable. Inevitable carries more drama: the outcome is built into the situation itself, and calling it inevitable often sounds resigned, as if everyone watched it coming.

certain: Certain means sure to happen — no doubt is left about the outcome. Inevitable says something stronger about why: no action by anyone can prevent it. Tomorrow's sunrise is certain; for a glass already tipping off the shelf, the crash is inevitable — nothing can stop it now.

inescapable: Inescapable means impossible to get away from, and it often describes what already surrounds you — an inescapable conclusion, inescapable summer heat. Inevitable points forward: an event that has not arrived yet but cannot be stopped. You are trapped in the inescapable; you are waiting for the inevitable.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

avoidable: able to be escaped or prevented

preventable: able to be stopped before it happens

Where it sits · how firmly the outcome is sealed

likely → inevitable → fated

likely vs. inevitable: Likely is weaker than inevitable — a likely event will probably happen, but an inevitable one cannot fail to happen.

fated vs. inevitable: Fated is stronger than inevitable — inevitable means nothing can stop it now, while fated suggests it was destined from the very beginning.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — in-: not (Latin)

root — evit-: to avoid, shun (Latin)

suffix — -able: able to be (Latin)

Put it together: Latin evitare meant 'to avoid.' Add -able ('can be done') and in- ('not'), and inevitable literally means 'not able to be avoided.'

Where This Word Comes From: Latin vitare ('to dodge, avoid') survives in English only inside inevitable and its close relatives. The Romans used evitare for sidestepping a blow; put in- ('not') in front and you have the thing no sidestep can save you from. If something is inevitable, there is simply no dodging it.
